status_reasoning: The first 3D EM structure of PRC2-AEBP2 is well-supported by appropriate methodology (RCT reconstruction, 39,527 particles, 21 Å resolution). The elongated architecture with 4 lobes and 2 arms is consistently observed across multiple reconstructions, indicating structural homogeneity. The exclusion of end-on views is a limitation but does not undermine the overall structural determination.

The reconstitution strategy and stabilization approach are well-documented. The tetrameric PRC2 showed conformational flexibility (C25), which was addressed by adding AEBP2 cofactor and mild glutaraldehyde cross-linking (0.015%). The improved quality of 2D class averages after cross-linking (C34) validates this approach. The biochemical homogeneity is confirmed by SDS-PAGE analysis.

The cross-linking/mass spectrometry interaction map is well-supported by appropriate methodology (isotope-labeled DSSG cross-linker, xQuest analysis). The cross-linking data are validated against known crystal structures (C43, C51), showing consistency. The identification of AEBP2 as a central interaction hub (C57) is supported by multiple independent cross-links. The extensive interactions are consistent with previous biochemical data (C56).

The localization of EED WD40 domain to Lobe A is well-supported by multiple independent tags (internal GFP at positions 115 and 370, plus MBP-Ezh2 N-terminus). The novel internal GFP tagging method successfully overcame limitations of terminal tags. The positioning is validated by consistency with known EED-Ezh2 crystal structure (C69) and allows accurate placement of the histone H3-binding site (C70).

The localization of RbAp48 WD40 domain to Lobe D is supported by indirect tagging via Suz12-GFP123, which exploits the known Suz12-RbAp48 interaction. The docking of Drosophila RbAp48-Suz12 crystal structure into the density shows high fidelity (C74). The inferred histone H3 tail orientation (C75) is a reasonable inference based on the docked structure, though it remains a model.

The localization of Ezh2 domains is well-supported by multiple internal GFP tags at strategic positions (after first SANT at 303, before second SANT at 436, flanking SET domain). The proximity of the two SANT domains is independently validated by cross-linking data (C78). The SET domain localization to Lobe B is consistent with cross-linking showing interactions with Suz12 and AEBP2 Zn fingers.

The Suz12 chain path is inferred from limited tagging data (Suz12-GFP269 and Suz12-ΔC-GFP). The N-terminus and C-terminus localizations are reasonable, but the proposed path through Arm2 (C81) is speculative. The authors acknowledge this with 'most likely,' indicating uncertainty. Additional tags along the Suz12 chain would strengthen this assignment.

The AEBP2 chain path is well-supported by multiple tags (GFP84, GFP115, C-terminal GFP) and extensive cross-linking data. The Zn finger localization near Lobe A/Arm 1 is validated by cross-links to EED and Ezh2 SANT1 (C83). The C-terminal localization is supported by cross-links to central Suz12 (C85). The opposite directionality relative to Suz12 (C86) is a reasonable inference from the combined data.

The stoichiometry determination (single copy of each subunit) is supported by observation of only one additional density per tagged complex across all labeling experiments. This is consistent with biochemical data showing stoichiometric complex by SDS-PAGE. The successful localization of all subunits confirms the structure contains all purified components.

The comprehensive architectural model is supported by convergent evidence from multiple orthogonal techniques: EM structure, cross-linking/MS, internal tagging, and integration with existing crystal structures. The redundancy and consistency across methods (C89) provides strong validation. This represents a significant advance over previous limited structural knowledge (two isolated domains).

The proposed allosteric role of AEBP2 (C7) is an interpretation based on its position and stabilization effect. While AEBP2 clearly acts as an interaction hub (C45, C57) and stabilizes the complex, the specific mechanism of allosteric regulation is not directly demonstrated. This remains a hypothesis requiring functional validation through mutagenesis or activity assays.

The localization of histone-tail binding regions (EED and RbAp48 WD40 domains) near the SET methyltransferase site is well-supported by the structural data. The EED H3-binding site at Lobe A/Arm 2 intersection (C70) and RbAp48 at Lobe D facing the SET domain provide a structural basis for chromatin-based regulation. The formation of a structural core (C102) is directly observed in the EM density.

The proposed regulatory mechanisms are reasonable inferences based on structural proximity and known SANT domain function (C104), but they remain mechanistic hypotheses. The proximity of SANT domains to the SET domain (C105) and VEFS to SET (C106) suggests potential regulatory interactions, but the actual allosteric mechanisms are not demonstrated. These models require functional validation through mutagenesis and activity assays.

The hypothesis that PRC2 can simultaneously bind two nucleosomes is based on the elongated shape and WD40 domain spacing (~16 nm matching di-nucleosome spacing of ~15 nm). While this is a reasonable structural inference supported by known substrate preference (C114), it remains speculative. Direct demonstration of di-nucleosome binding in the context of the full complex structure would be needed for full support.

These claims about the utility and implications of the structural model are appropriate forward-looking statements. The structure does provide a framework for interpreting previous biochemical data (C118) and generates testable hypotheses (C119). The expectation of conservation across higher eukaryotes (C120) is reasonable given sequence similarity, though this is a prediction rather than a demonstrated result.
